issues.item: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
issues.explanation: 'Catastrophising Others' is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile and the trauma type. The other items center on childhood physical abuse, mistrust, touch-sensitivity, fragmented memory, guilt, and self-damage; obsessive worry about harm befalling loved ones points to a different threat theme and is not supported by the appraisals or memory content.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' suggests a home-intrusion/security threat theme. In this profile, threat is otherwise expressed as interpersonal danger cues (unexpected touch, ominous silence) linked to caregiver abuse. Without matching appraisals or memory content about break-ins or external intruders, this item is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected items.

vignette: Arthur Vance had spent decades convincing himself that his temperament was fundamentally broken, a conviction that first took root in the years following his father's escalating rages. Believing himself permanently changed for the worse by the childhood abuse, he stopped allowing himself to process the past and instead fell into a cycle of dwelling on what his father had done, then punishing himself for what he believed he had done wrong to deserve it. This rigid mental habit became his only way to navigate loss of control, anchoring his daily existence in a loop of resentment and self-reproach. That same conviction warped how his body read the present. Because he was certain people could not be trusted, any unannounced contact-like a tailor's measuring tape snapping near his ribs or a colleague's hand landing on his shoulder at the pattern-cutting table-triggered a jolt of pure alarm that left his breath catching and his shoulders locking. His distrust did not stay abstract; it manifested as a physical startle that made collaboration nearly impossible in his Greenwich Village studio. His fractured worldview also dictated how the past arrived in his mind. Convinced that his nervous system was broken beyond repair, Arthur found that when memories surfaced, they refused to cohere into a linear timeline; instead, they shattered into disjointed fragments he could never piece together, leaving him unable to tell a clear story of what happened even to himself. The lack of narrative structure felt like proof that his mind was simply failing him. Those fragmented recollections, in turn, flooded his workspace with phantom warnings. When a sudden draft silenced the hum of his industrial sewing machines, the empty quiet would pull the disjointed memories forward, and his body would immediately tense, convinced that something dangerous was about to happen. The memories did not just return; they hijacked his present-moment safety. The terror of those unspooling memories reinforced his core beliefs about his own deterioration. Every time he stared at a photograph and felt a hollow, numb detachment-as if watching a stranger's life unfold on a screen-his inability to feel the expected grief or anger confirmed his fear that he was losing his grip on reality. His own physiological state then scrambled his ability to access the past at all. The constant readiness to bolt whenever his posture went rigid meant that any attempt to review old journals was met with a wall of panic, leaving him unable to retrieve or integrate the events without his thoughts fracturing further. That relentless readiness also cemented his worst interpretations. The way his heart hammered against his ribs whenever he stood alone in his now-empty loft convinced him that his own body was plotting against him, teaching him to view his nervous system not as an overprotective alarm, but as a traitor confirming his permanent damage. His relentless rumination, meanwhile, eroded his capacity to make sense of what occurred. By obsessively replaying arguments with his stepfather and his own perceived childhood failures, Arthur drowned out the few coherent details that might have emerged, ensuring that his trauma remained a tangled knot rather than a processed memory. Finally, this endless mental circling solidified his despair. When he exhausted himself analyzing the violence he survived, the emotional hangover left him certain that he was beyond repair, transforming temporary distress into a fixed belief that his reactions since the event meant he was going crazy. Arthur Vance is a fifty-five-year-old fashion designer whose once-bustling atelier now sits half-finished, garments draped over mannequins like unspoken accusations. Over the past two years, the combination of avoiding bed and sleepless nights, coupled with feeling on guard even inside his own home, has bled into his livelihood. He now refuses to work after dusk, claiming the twilight makes his nerves twitch, and he has fired three assistants who tried to hand him tools without verbal warning. Divorced and isolated, he was finally driven to seek help after a recent fitting: when a client reached out to touch his wrist, Arthur recoiled so violently he knocked over a rack of silk bolts. The sudden guilt on recall when the memories briefly broke through had been paralyzing. He came to my office hoping to stop the panic attacks and quiet the relentless loops in his head, terrified that if he stops fighting the memories, he will finally lose his mind entirely.
